No short answers for you, buddy. You need to know this shit for life: The only 2 things you can significantly change are amount of muscle and body fat %. Most of the fat is stored under the skin, so if you don't look "toned up" chances are you could be leaner. In order to do that, eat less than what you spend. As long as you eat enough protein and some fat and fiber, you won't lose muscle (which would be counterproductive to your appearance and health).

If being lean isn't enough, then you need hypertrophy (muscle gain). For that you still need the protein (at least 0.8 times your lb weight in grams, every day) and progressive overload. In that regard, yoga is very, very inferior to weight lifting and calisthenics.

Actually that was your question. "Toning up" = getting leaner. Toning up is a made up term. It's not intense, it can only give you some muscle if you don't have any.

Isometric exercise is known as a great way to build strength and muscle size. Yoga will make you more muscular and very strong and its not just for "toning".

"Isometrics increases muscle size AND strength; the two aren't mutually exclusive. When you increase strength, you increase muscle mass and connective tissue strength, but the way that the muscle grows will be different for each case. There is myofibrillar growth, in which the muscle itself actually increases in size and protein density. This reinforces the muscle, making it much stronger. The dense muscle of martial artists, powerlifters, and the like is often indicative of myofibrillar growth.

There is also sarcoplasmic growth, which increases the amount of water and glucose around the muscle cells; because of the extra water and sugar, the muscle make have more endurance, but its overall contractile strength doesn't improve. Bodybuilders are usually a prime example of sarcoplasmic growth. (Granted, you have to have some myofibrillar growth to achieve sufficient sarcoplasmic growth.)"

Well this particular model (myofibrillar vs. sarcoplasmic hypertrophy) may have some scientific basis but it's completely irrelevant to the average Joe/Jane and I'll tell you why.

You'll gain muscle in any kind of progressive overload, given proper rest and sufficient protein intake. In sports you control only intensity and duration (running, lifting, etc) there's no evidence whatsoever that training going either way would affect the proportion of myo and sarco. Meaning you can't control it, just like you can't lower fat "just in the abs". You lower body fat, so that you just have less fat overall to be distributed so abs get lower.

This myth probably came from the difference in powerlifters and bodybuilders training, mass and strength. There are several factors, but the main one is that training volume (total reps x load) is by evidence and consensus the main aspect of hypertrophy. By increasing the load, you have to drastically lower your number of reps and you have to rest more (ex: for 5 reps, if you lower load by a mere 20%, you could do around 10 reps for the same exercise and you could spend less time resting for the next 10 meaning higher loads lead to lower training volume). On the other hand, higher load leads to CNS improvements (not myo) which contribute to strength more so than amount of muscle. Point is: The muscle gained (at a lower rate if you only train on higher loads) is the same for the same athlete in different training programs.

Don't take my word for it. You can find plenty of studies on training volume relation to hypertrophy and this CNS stuff is also very well documented. Regardless, this distinction between powerlifters and bodybuilders in changing because it's beneficial to PLs to add volume training, and likewise to BBs to add strength training.
